note: 頭 do → du: the initial is direct; o and u are not separable at the ~50% vowel recovery §7 reports. 曼 mɑn → man: exact, and the coda -n is written, because -n is one of the six codas the Chinese syllable can carry. One vowel change in two syllables. The rival reading tümen needs ü, which the Later Han script cannot write at all. duman / tuman / touman “smoke, fog, mist” is one word across Kāşgarî, the Codex Cumanicus and modern Turkish. The standard identification is tümen “ten thousand”, which is absent from the Cuman vocabulary entirely.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: The frame is b/m – k/g – t/d – nasal or stop, and both codas are written, which makes it one of the tightest frames in the record and also one of the least determinate, because neither character has a single value. 冒 has two Later Han readings, mək and mouᶜ; 頓 has tuənᶜ and tuət, and a third value from the commentarial note 頓音毒, reported by Pulleyblank as Early Middle Chinese dawk, which is a substitution recorded by a commentator rather than a row of the table. 冒 mək → bögü: the m- stands for a source b-, 3 of 22 in the Later Han corpus, 13.6%; the written -k stands for the source g; and the final vowel is not written, one character covering two source syllables, a device found in 47 of the 1,017 verified pairs, as 竭 covers -gata in tathāgata. There is a character-level precedent as well as a rate: 冒 and 默 share the reading mək and 默啜 is read Bögü-Çor, while 牟 mu writes the same word in 牟羽 for the Uyghur Bögü Qaghan. 頓 → tuğ: a velar-final second element, which the corpus writes with the -t coda of 頓's second row in 2 of 21 opportunities and with the -k of the substitution in 10 of 21, and never with the -n of the first row, 0 of 21. Bögü Tuğ, “sage standard”. tuğ is the horse-tail or yak-tail standard carried on a pole, attested in Old Turkic (tuğ taşıkar “when the standard went out”, Moyun Çor, cited by Doerfer at ETY I 170) and glossed by Kāşgarî as the drum and banner borne before the king, with toquz tuğluğ xan “a khan of nine standards”. bögü is a regnal epithet across the record: Teŋri Bögü Teŋriken, Bögü Qaghan of the Uyghurs, Bögü-Çor of the Türks; Kāşgarî glosses bügü as “bilgin, akıllı, hakim” and Clauson says it “seems to connote both wisdom and mysterious spiritual power”. Both halves are attested independently of any Chinese source and two nouns in apposition is the commonest Turkic name pattern. Why a velar-final second element. Of the three values 頓 can take, two admit a velar-final element, one admits the liquid-final Baγatur the field has read for a century, and one admits a nasal-final one. §9.2 of the paper sets out that comparison and does not choose; the preference here is this author's. What is not settled. The loan direction of tuğ is disputed: Doerfer's TMEN 969 gives it as a loan from Chinese, which would put it out of reach of a name of the early second century BC, while his own addendum in volume IV quotes Menges (1968: 169, as cited there) that the Chinese word “might well be an ancient loanword in Chinese” and Franke (letter of 23 March 1966) that the Chinese word is first attested in the Zhouli and is “kaum jünger als 2. Jh. v. Chr.”. A ninth-century check adds nothing either way, and is recorded so that it is not made twice: Tekin’s glossary to the Irk Bitig has the verb tug- “to rise (of sun)” but not the noun, the text’s word for a flag is uçrug, and bögü is not in it. That text is sixty-five omens and a few hundred words, so absence from it is not evidence of anything. The reading is also ordinary on the substitution, marginal on 頓's second row and excluded on the first, which is the row printed here; the compound is not itself attested, only its halves; and the frame does not fix the vowel of the second syllable. The rival reading carries its own difficulties, recorded in S1.4. Full discussion in S1.4.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper. §9.2 prices the three values 頓 can take and does not choose among them; the loan direction of tuğ is disputed

note: 稽 kʰei → ki: an aspirated velar is the ordinary vehicle for a source k, and the diphthong ei for i is routine. 粥 tśuk → çük: tś- is the default character class for a source affricate (37% in the Sanskrit corpus), and the coda -k is actually written, the strongest part of the reading, since a stop coda goes unwritten 30% of the time. Only ü is unavailable and surfaces as u. kiçig / kiçik / kiçük “small, younger” is attested three times independently: Kāşgarî has kiçik and kiçük with the derivative kiçiglik, the Kutadgu Bilig has kiçig oğlan erken “when he was a small boy” (1823), and the Codex has Kečak glossed paucus. 稽粥 is the personal name of Laoshang chanyu, Modu's son and successor, so “the younger” fits the succession the Chinese sources record.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 軍 kun → kün: initial and coda direct; ü is unwritable and surfaces as u. 臣 dźin → çin: dź is the voiced partner of tś, and voicing is leaky in both directions in every corpus measured, so a source ç is reachable through it; the -n coda is written. kün “sun, day”. The Seljuk regnal names Kaykhusraw and Kayqubad carry an association of royal solar radiance through their kay- element.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 伊 ʔi → i: a glottal onset is the standard way to write a vowel-initial syllable. 稚 ḍi → di: retroflex ḍ for d is routine. 斜 ja → ya: this character class emits ya more strongly than any other single-syllable correspondence in the record. All three steps are default. idi “lord, master”, attested in Old Turkic. Compare Murad I's epithet Hüdavendigâr, “the sovereign”, a title of the same shape and force.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 烏 ʔɑ → a: vowel-initial, direct. 維 wi → bı is the weak step: the Chinese character carries a w-, and while Turkic b- and w- alternate, the transcription reads more naturally as avı than abı. This is one of only five items in the record decoded entirely from character-specific evidence, so the mismatch cannot be attributed to a gap in the data. av “hunt”, avcı “hunter”. Avcı names an occupation; abı is proposed as naming a trait. Avcı is also the epithet of Mehmed IV.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 詹 tśam → çam: tś- is the default affricate spelling and the -m coda is written. 師 ṣi → şı: the retroflex sibilant is the standard vehicle for ş. 廬 liɑ → lı: note that Chinese l- also carries source r-: in the paper's correspondence counts an r- was written l- in 12 of 14 attestations, so this syllable is genuinely ambiguous between -lı and -rı. The same solar association proposed for Künçin, from a stem of shining or dazzling.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 呴 huo → ka, 犁 lei → lı, 湖 gɑ → k: three onsets, each taken from the majority correspondence, with nothing inserted and no coda discarded. The velar class covers h-, k- and g- alike, so the first and third syllables cost nothing. Kāşgarî glosses kalık “hava, gök, sema” (air, sky, heaven). The word belongs to the same semantic field as 撑犁, the one Xiongnu term the Chinese sources gloss (天 “heaven”), so a ruler bearing it would not be isolated in the record. A second exact fit, kılık “disposition, manner”, is available if the sky reading is thought too convenient.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 且 tsɑ → ça: ts- for a source affricate is a minority spelling but a real one, 15% in the Sanskrit corpus and 9% in Ligeti. 鞮 te → tı: direct. 侯 go → gka asks a single Chinese syllable to carry a consonant cluster it structurally cannot, so the reading adds material the transcription does not have. çat- “to strike together, to clash”. Compare Selçuk Bey, whose name has been read as “perpetually ready for the fight”.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 姑 kɑ → ga is well supported by the velar correspondence. The other two syllables are not: 狐 ɣuɑ → kur supplies an -r that Later Han has no coda slot for, and 鹿 lok → lu discards a coda that was written. Adding an unwritable segment and dropping a written one in the same word pulls in opposite directions. 狐鹿姑 captured the Han general Li Guangli and held the confederation together through a hard decade, so an epithet of binding fits the record. Compare the Göktürk ruler Kapgan Kagan, kapgan “the encloser”.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 壺 gɑ → ka: given a Later Han voiced g-, the source sound is more often k than g, so the devoicing is normal rather than a liberty. 衍 jan → yan: direct, coda written. 鞮 te → tı: direct. All three steps are default or better, phonetically one of the cleaner readings here. kay- “to slide, to slip away”. Parallel in sense to Bayezid I's Yıldırım: a natural force taken as a regnal epithet.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 虛 kʰɨɑ → ka, 閭 liɑ → l, 權 gyan → kan: the first three characters match exactly, including the written -n coda, at zero minority steps. Only 渠 gɨɑ is left unaccounted for, and it may carry a separate title element. kalkan “shield” is in Kāşgarî and in the Codex Cumanicus as Kalkani, “scutum ejus”. A weapon or armour name is an ordinary steppe formation, and it needs no compound to be read.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

proposed_sense: blessed sovereign of the arrow flank
note: 握 ʔɔk → ok is exact, with the -k coda written, and 衍 jan → yan and 鞮 te → tı are direct. The weak point is 朐 guo → kutuğ, which expands one Chinese syllable into two Turkic ones; nothing in the corpora licenses that expansion. ok “arrow” doubles as a division of the confederation in later Turkic usage (the On Ok, “ten arrows”, of the Western Turks) which is what makes a territorial reading available. kut is “heavenly favour, fortune”.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 呼 hɑ → ka: an h/k substitution, which the Mongolian corpus supports strongly (a source k or q was written with an h- character 27% of the time). 韓 gɑn → gan: exact, coda written. 邪 ja → ya: the strongest single correspondence in the record. The written sequence ha gan ya becomes ka-gan-ya on one change. 呼韓邪 commanded the left flank before becoming ruler, so the Chinese record itself supplies the office that the reading names.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

proposed_sense: border-maker, one who carves the boundary
note: 郅 tśit → çit: tś- is the default affricate vehicle and the -t coda is written. 支 tśe → çi: default. Both syllables use the majority correspondence and neither requires an inserted or deleted segment. çit / çiz-, of marking or carving a boundary. 郅支 broke away westward and set up a rival seat, so a name of division fits the career, though it is equally possible that the career suggested the name.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 若 ńɑk → ınak: a palatal nasal onset with the -k coda written. 鞮 te → -t: the final stop is not written, and Table 7 of the paper licenses that at 30%. One objection stands and the paper states it: if the source was ınakt, the opening ı- is not written and 若鞮 has no room for it. One of the two readings argued in the paper itself, at §9, and it is listed here so this supplement can be read as a single list with the standard visible in it. Inak is glossed fidelis “faithful” in the Codex Cumanicus; the Hou Hanshu glosses 若鞮 as 孝 “filial”; the plural in -t is an Old Turkic formation used with titles (tegin → tegit); and Clauson records Chagatay inak as “a royal representative or senior minister”, so a court title on this root is what the word ordinarily does.
status: argued in §9 of the paper; one of the two readings in this file that meet the paper's standard

note: 復株累 buk ṭio lui → büktel: the b-, the -k coda, the dental and the liquid all fall in place across the three characters, at zero minority steps, with only the front rounded vowel unwritable. One attested word covers the whole prefix rather than an invented two-element compound. 若鞮 → Inakt is treated in §S1.4. Kāşgarî gives büktel as “orta boylu; yassı arkalı, oturamaklı”: of middling height and flat-backed. A name from a bodily description is a well-attested Turkic type; compare the Hungarian royal name Şişman.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

proposed_sense: the yellow, the fair, of the Inakt
note: 搜 so → sar: a sibilant onset, which the correspondence counts make obligatory: a source k, q or g was written with a Chinese sibilant in 0 of 2,124 attestations, while Chinese sibilant characters transcribe s, š, č or ś in 98% of 837 cases. The final -r is not written and could not be: Later Han carries no -r in any coda position. 諧 gɛi → ıg: a velar onset, direct. Nothing is inserted, and no character is read as a sound it cannot carry. 若鞮 → Inakt is treated in §S1.4. sarıg “sarı, sarı renk” (yellow) is in Kāşgarî, and survives as modern Turkish Sarı, still current both as a name and as an epithet. Color epithets are a documented Turkic naming type: the same dictionary has çakır “grey-eyed”, and Çal “dappled, grey” is proposed for 烏珠留若鞮 on the same footing. Ninety-one attested headwords fit this two-syllable frame, so it does not determine the reading; sarıg is offered as the most plausible of them, with nothing in the transcription standing against it.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

proposed_sense: Arrow of High Eminence, of the Inakt
note: 車 tśʰa → çöge: the aspirated affricate is a good vehicle for ç, but ö is unwritable and a second syllable is added. 牙 ŋa → ok: a velar-nasal initial standing for a vowel-initial syllable is unsupported. çöge of height or eminence, with the same ok element.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

proposed_sense: the grey or dappled one, of the Inakt
note: 烏 ʔɑ is vowel-initial, so the reading begins at 珠 tśo → ç, with 留 liu → l: an affricate written with the default tś- character and a liquid, both majority correspondences. Nothing is inserted, and no character is read as a consonant it does not carry. çal is “alaca, kır” in Kāşgarî: dappled, grey. Color epithets are a persistent Turkic naming pattern, as çakır “grey-eyed” shows in the same dictionary.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 烏 ʔɑ → u: a glottal-onset character is the standard way to write a vowel-initial syllable. 累 lui → lu: a liquid, direct. Two characters, two segments, nothing supplied that the transcription does not carry. The Codex Cumanicus glosses Oulu as magnus. Uluğ “great” is among the most common elements in Turkic titulature, which is both the strength of this reading and its weakness: a very common word is an easy target to hit.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

later_han: hɑ tɑ ńə śi douᴮ kou ńɑk te
turkish_render: ha ta nyı şi dou kou nyak te
note: Eight characters, and correspondingly the least constrained reading in the file: the longer the string, the more ways there are to split it into Turkic elements, and the split itself is doing most of the work rather than any individual correspondence. 呼 hɑ → öz and 皋 kou → uluğ are the two largest jumps. öz “self, core” and uluğ “great”, both common Old Turkic elements in titulature.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 攣 lyan → el moves the liquid from the onset of the Chinese syllable to the coda of the Turkic one; no corpus shows that kind of metathesis. 鞮 te → indi expands one syllable into two. The reading is driven by the sense rather than by the transcription. el “realm, state” with the definite past in -di: literally “he founded the realm”. This is the clan name as the Shiji and Hanshu write it.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

proposed_sense: state founder of the rocky region
note: 虛 kʰɨɑ → kıya is reachable. 連 lianᴮ → lığ adds an unwritten coda, and 題 de → el-indi carries a whole two-syllable word on one character. Three characters are being asked to yield five syllables. The same clan name as 攣鞮, in the form the Hou Hanshu gives, with the kaya element recurring from 虛閭權渠.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

proposed_sense: army commander; the earlier form of çavuş
note: Two characters, 單 with a written coda and 于 open. 單 → çar- takes the second of the character’s two Later Han readings, the dental tɑn, for the onset: a source voiceless affricate written with the voiced dź- of the first reading is 0 of 48 in the Sanskrit corpus, while with a dental onset it is 8 of 48, 16.7%. For the coda it takes the Old Chinese value, Baxter and Sagart’s *dar, whose liquid becomes the -n of the later table; step 43 measures how often the two reconstructions differ in this way across the record. 于 wɑ → -vuş is the best value this character offers: a source v written with a Chinese w- character is 9 of 65, 13.8%, against 1 of 55 for a source b and 0 of 140 for a vowel-initial syllable. The final -ş is unwritten, which a sibilant coda is in 27 of 36 cases, 75%, since Later Han has no sibilant coda. The liquid is what makes the form possible. Across the 8,930 headwords of the Kāşgarî index and the Codex, -rv- and -rb- occur 18 times in native words (burba-, karva-, kurbaka, turbı), while -nv- occurs 0 times and -nb- 5 times, all in loanwords: a liquid before a labial is Turkic, a nasal before one is not. Two shapes the frame excludes outright, whatever word is tried. A velar first element is not available: a voiced affricate writing a velar stop appears once in 220 in the Sanskrit corpus and that one case is a translation mislabelled as a transcription, and characters that write kan exactly, 干 kɑn and 汗 gɑnᶜ, were available and not used. A vowel-initial second element is not available either: a glide character writing a vowel-initial source syllable is 0 of 140. Çarvuş, the earlier form of çavuş, “army commander”. A native Turkic title of the first rank. Clauson does not mark it foreign, unlike beg, xan and xağan, and Doerfer 1055 has it travelling outward, to Persian and thence to Urdu and Lezgian. It is attested in the eighth-century inscriptions in the highest possible company: bilgesi çavuşı erti, “he was his Counsellor and Army Commander” (Ix. 17), and at Tonyukuk 7 the speaker is Tonyukuk himself. Clauson glosses it “originally the principal military officer of a xağan, the military counterpart of bilge”, and adds that “as time went on the post gradually lost status”, ending as the modern Turkish sergeant; Kāşgarî defines the office as the one who orders the ranks in battle and restrains the troops from outrages (I 368), and his form of the word is çaβuş, with a bilabial fricative. Why it is proposed here. Founders of dynasties commonly bear military titles: Osman Gazi, Alp Arslan, Alp Tegin. And a supreme title that began as a military one is an ordinary trajectory, as with Latin imperator “commander” and dux. The Türk inscriptions are a thousand years later than the Xiongnu, so the decline Clauson describes was already under way when they were cut, and at the earlier stage the office Clauson calls the principal military officer of a xağan could have been the ruler’s own title rather than his officer’s. What is not settled. Çarvuş itself is not recorded in the later Turkic sources. Clauson’s Etymological Dictionary, Erdal’s Grammar of Old Turkic, Kāşgarî’s Dīwān, the Kutadgu Bilig, Doerfer’s TMEN and Tekin’s edition of the Irk Bitig all carry çavuş or çaβuş and none carries a form with the liquid. Abū Ḥayyān’s Kitāb al-İdrāk is not among them: the only copy held is the Arabic-script scan, whose OCR its own pages rate at about a third accurate, so it cannot be searched either way. On this reading the -r- was lost before the eighth century, which is a thousand years after the name was written down.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper. The reading takes the second Later Han reading of 單 for the onset and its Old Chinese value for the coda; çarvuş itself is not recorded in the later Turkic sources, which carry çavuş

later_han: ḍaŋ lei kuɑ dɑ dźan wɑ
turkish_render: dang lei kua da can va
note: Six characters forming the full ceremonial title, and the only item in the record the Chinese sources gloss in full. It decomposes into three units that each have their own row here: 撑犁 ḍaŋ lei, 孤塗 kuɑ dɑ and 單于 dźan wɑ. No separate reading is proposed for the compound; whatever the three parts are read as, the whole follows. The Hanshu glosses the phrase as “Son of Heaven, the Chanyu”, with 撑犁 = 天 “heaven” and 孤塗 = 子 “son”. That makes it the single most valuable item in the record, because both the form and the meaning are recorded, and it is the evidence on which most of the language-attribution argument has rested for a century.
status: compound; read through its three constituent rows

note: 撑 ḍaŋ → tang: retroflex ḍ for t is routine and the -ŋ coda is written. 犁 lei → lı: direct. Both steps are default. The same two syllables equally support tengri, which the Chinese gloss 天 and the lexicon search of §6.3 both favour: Kāşgarî returns it 4th, the Codex 2nd. tang of dawn or light, read as “bearing divine light; sacred”. Offered as an alternative to the standard identification with tengri, not as an improvement on it.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

proposed_sense: the blessing of heaven, with the third-person possessive
note: 孤 kuɑ → ku: the default velar onset, direct, with the coda open. 塗 dɑ → tı: a dental onset carrying the -t of kut, with the vowel free. Two characters, two syllables, nothing inserted and nothing discarded. The frame is k/g/h – t/d and both codas are unwritten, so a source -r, -l, -s or -z could hide in either. 66 attested headwords fit it. kutı, “the blessing of heaven”, with -ı as the third-person possessive. kut is the divine favour that legitimises a ruler: Clauson records it in the hendiadys kut kıv “divine favour”, and it is the word the Kutadgu Bilig is named from. The possessive is not padding but what Turkic requires of the second noun in a genitive-possessive phrase, tengri kutı, “the kut of heaven”, which is the shape of the full title 撑犁孤塗單于. The phrase is attested, not assembled. Clauson's entry for kut cites the Irk Bitig for teŋri kutınta “by the favour of heaven”, which is teŋri kutı with a locative on it, and the Orkhon inscriptions for the dative kutıŋa, in the passage where the ruler's mother is said to have enjoyed the favour of heaven. So both the possessive form and the two-word phrase are on record in Old Turkic, and the Chinese title maps onto them element for element. That is now checkable in the primary edition rather than only in Clauson’s report of it: Tekin’s glossary to the Irk Bitig carries kut as a headword, glossed “divine favor, blessing, good fortune”, and its citations include kutınta at omens 15 and 56, the first of them in the phrase teŋri kutınta. The manuscript is ninth-century. In Old Turkic that suffix is -ı / -i, so kutı rather than kutu; the -u of modern Turkish kutu comes from labial harmony, a later development. The two-character spelling is itself evidence for the second syllable. Had the word been a bare kut, a single character was available that writes it exactly, 骨 kuət, with the -t on the page, and the record uses that character in 骨都侯. A scribe who had the one-syllable option and wrote two characters was writing two syllables. The vowel of 塗 is ɑ and matches neither ı nor u closely, but §7 of the paper puts vowel recovery at 50.0% with the interval straddling one half, so the vowel is the least informative part of the spelling and cannot decide between them. The Chinese gloss is 子 “son”, and this reading does not translate it. That is recorded against the proposal rather than explained away. The word the gloss wants is oğul, and oğul is barred by the writing rather than merely disfavoured: it is vowel-initial while 孤 carries a velar, and in the Sanskrit corpus a source vowel-initial syllable took a zero or glottal onset in 96% of 183 cases and a velar in none of them. Its medial -ğ- has nowhere to sit either, since 塗 is dental. So oğul is not one of the 66 headwords that fit the frame and never was a candidate; the same wall excluded okluk at 胡祿. Of the 66 that do fit, none means “son”: they include kut “heavenly favour, fortune”, kat “layer”, kata “time, occasion”, ketü, Kerti verus and kötü. The Yeniseian rival, as its author now leaves it. Pulleyblank compared the word with Arin bïkjàl “son”. In 2000 Vovin held that Arin form to be isolated in the family, the other languages reflecting Proto-Yeniseian *puʔ-b “son” (Ket hiʔp, Yug fiʔp, Kott fup), and found no Altaic etymology either (Vovin 2000, CAJ 44/1, p. 91); an earlier draft of this supplement cited him for that. He withdrew it three years later: “I would like to take back my suggestion that Arin form is isolated in Yeniseian” (Vovin 2003, Part 2). He then rebuilds the comparison rather than dropping it, reading Pumpokol p-halla “my son” as a cluster with the first-person prefix rather than as an f-, which makes it cognate with the Arin form, and ruling out Pulleyblank’s Ket qal/qaloq instead. The Yeniseian side of this item is therefore stronger than an earlier draft of this supplement said, and it is recorded here as he left it. So this is the one item in the record where two independent kinds of evidence point at different words: the writing supports kutı and the gloss asks for a word the writing excludes. The gloss can be accounted for without supposing the informant was confused about Xiongnu. If the title meant “the heaven-favoured chanyu”, the Chinese expression that fits it is 天子, “Son of Heaven”, which is their own imperial title. 天子 has two characters where the Xiongnu title has two words, so the element glosses follow mechanically from that equation: 撑犁 aligns with 天 and 孤塗 with 子. On that account the first gloss is a true lexical gloss, since 撑犁 is teŋri “heaven”, and the second is a back-formation from the phrase-level equivalence rather than testimony about what 孤塗 means. This is an explanation of the gloss and not a test of it, which is why the reading is offered here rather than argued in the paper.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper. The transcription raises no objection; the Chinese gloss 子 'son' does, and the word that gloss wants, ogul, is excluded by the writing

proposed_sense: lady; a woman related by marriage
note: 閼 ʔɑt → el-: a vowel-initial character whose written -t carries the source liquid. Later Han had no -r or -l in any coda, so a source syllable ending in one was written with a -t or left open: of 37 such syllables in the Sanskrit corpus, 21 were left open and 14 took a -t, 38%. 氏 dźeᴮ → -ti: a dental onset with the vowel free. The first character is not polyphonic: Schuessler’s table gives 閼 the single value ʔɑt, and Baxter and Sagart give Middle Chinese ʔat from Old Chinese *qˤat. The -n that the parallel spelling 焉支 carries belongs to 焉, a different character, which Baxter and Sagart give two readings, both in -n. The second character is another matter: the table gives 氏 as dźeᴮ, gieᴮ, tśe and kie, and Baxter and Sagart reconstruct *k.deʔ with a velar preinitial, which is where the velar readings come from. An earlier draft of this supplement called this item fully character-anchored; that is true of the emission row and overstates the constraint on the second character. Elti, “lady”. Modern Turkish elti is what each of two brothers’ wives calls the other, and in dialect what two wives of one man call each other. It is not only modern: Clauson records élti: glossed “lady”, standing opposite al-jāriya “slave girl”, in a fourteenth-century Arabic-Turkish glossary, which is the sense a consort’s title would want. Nişanyan takes Middle Turkic élti “married woman, as a respectful term” and derives it, with a stated doubt, from Old Turkic élt- “to carry, to lead”. If that holds, the word has the shape of kelin “bride”, which Clauson derives from kel- as “one who comes in (to the family)”: a deverbal noun naming a woman by how she entered it. 閼氏 is the title of the chanyu’s principal consort. Why this replaces the earlier proposal in this supplement. The earlier reading was ece “elder sister”, later eci “senior woman, lady”, both of which are in the Kāşgarî index (I, 86 and I, 87) and the second of which is the better semantic fit. Both discard the written -t of 閼, and the corpus makes that expensive: where the source has a single affricate or sibilant between two vowels, the preceding character was open in 134 of 143 junctions, 93.7%, and carried a -t in 2, 1.4%. That is a worse cost than the 1 in 37 the paper uses in §8.1 against a rival reading elsewhere, so consistency required either conceding it or finding a reading that uses the -t. elti uses it, at 38%. The earlier proposal is recorded here rather than removed, since the reasoning that led away from it is the useful part. What is not settled. elti is not in the Türk Dil Kurumu index nor in the Codex Cumanicus, and the fourteenth-century attestation is in the edition Clauson marks “(only)”. Pulleyblank read the title as Turkic and Mongolian qatun; Vovin rejects that and proposes instead a Yeniseian *alte or *elte “wife”, from Proto-Yeniseian *ʔal(V)it- (Kott alit, Assan alit, Arin biqam-alte), noting that it “could be transcribed in Chinese only as *ʔat-tej or *ʔen-tej”. He is right about the Chinese and the same spelling writes elti by the same steps, so the transcription does not choose between the two languages. §9.1 of the paper sets that out as a measured case of the negative result of §6.1.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper. Replaces an earlier ece / eci, which discarded the written -t of 閼; the same spelling also writes Vovin's Yeniseian *elte, which §9.1 measures

note: 屠 dɑ → do: a dental onset, direct. 耆 gɨ → ğru: a velar onset, with the -r unwritten, which is forced rather than permitted, since Later Han carries no -r in any coda position. 144 attested headwords fit the frame, so the transcription does little to narrow the choice; the vowels are free as always. Not our reading. The Turkic-hypothesis literature reads 屠耆 as *toγrï, and the Codex Cumanicus has Togru glossed rectus. The Chinese sources gloss 屠耆 as 賢 “worthy, wise”, and it appears in 左右屠耆王, the Wise Kings of the Left and Right. The senses meet more closely than “straight” suggests. Clauson derives toğuru: / toğru: as a gerund of toğur-, physically “straight” and then metaphorically “straight, honest, upright, true”, and that moral sense is old rather than modern: a fourteenth-century glossary renders it with Arabic al-tiqa “trustworthy, honest”, and toğru ayt- with ṣadaqa “to tell the truth”. The word survives across the whole Turkic family and as modern Turkish doğru, “straight, correct”. Toğrıl and Toğrul are not offered in support. The two names resemble toğru in sound, and they are well attested: Kāşgarî records that men are called Toğrıl, an Alp Toğrul Tégin appears in a Uyghur list of proper names, and the first Seljuk sultan bore the name. But Toğrıl is a bird of prey, and Clauson derives it from toğra- rather than from toğur-, noting that it never survived as a common noun. What makes the two look like one word is a separate homophone, the passive toğrıl- “to be upright”, which is from toğur- and survives as modern Turkish doğrul-. So the names are recorded here to head that resemblance off, not to rest anything on it: the case for Doğru stands on the Chinese gloss 賢 and on the attested moral sense of toğru. §9.1 of the paper tests this case alongside 徑路.
status: comparison cited in the literature, not ours; tested in §9.1 and supported

note: 谷 kok → körk: the default velar onset, with the -k coda written and the -r- unwritten before it. Later Han has no -r coda, so a source -rk cannot be written at all without spending a further character on an l- syllable; leaving it unwritten is the only option two characters allow, and it is the majority practice: step 31 counts 63 verified pairs whose source form has a liquid before a consonant, and the liquid is unwritten in 54 of them, 86% (達磨 for dharma, 薩達摩 for saddharma, 播鉢吒 for parpaṭa). In 6 of the 63, 10%, the scribe spent a further character carrying an l- onset instead, so the step this reading asks for has a measured minority against it rather than none. 蠡 leᴮ → lü: the l- onset direct, with an open coda. Two characters, two syllables, one unwritten consonant. Both are polyphonic characters: the table gives 谷 as kok, jok and lok, and 蠡 as leᴮ and loiᴮ; this reading takes the first of each. Körklü, “glorious, imposing”. The word is a headword in both lexicons used here: Kāşgarî has körklüg, glossed iyi, güzel ve gösterişli, “good, beautiful and imposing”, and the Codex Cumanicus has körk glossed decus, glory or dignity rather than prettiness. Clauson records the form across the whole span, with Kipchak and Coman körklü / körkli and Osmanlı görklü. The Kipchak form matters for the spelling: körklü carries no final -g, so the open coda of 蠡 is simply correct and nothing further needs licensing. The word is used of exalted figures and not only of pretty objects: an Old Turkic Buddhist text has teŋridem kız azu teŋri oğlanı teg körkle oğlan, “a child as beautiful as a divine girl or a son of God” (TT V 12, 127, via Clauson). Two caveats belong with that citation: Clauson calls the text a fairly late one, and he queries whether the -le form körkle / körtle is native rather than borrowed. The form this reading uses, körklüg, is not in doubt, being a straightforward derivation in -lüg from the attested körk. An authority assigns 谷 a different reading in this very title. Pulleyblank's Lexicon, at K1202a, glosses 谷 read lu as “luli king, Xiongnu title”, cross-referring gu and yu as the other readings. That is the lok branch, on which no Turkic word can fill the first syllable at all, so if Pulleyblank is right this reading is not available and 谷蠡 is not a Turkic word. The proposal is recorded with that against it, unresolved. The other readings of 谷 do not compete. On lok, which the office's conventional name, the Luli Kings, would suggest, the first syllable begins with a Chinese l-, and a Chinese l- writes a source l- or r-. Turkic admits neither initially: Clauson calls initial r-, like initial l-, a sound entirely foreign to the language, and loanwords that established themselves took a prosthetic vowel. That branch yields no candidates at all, so if 谷 is lok here, 谷蠡 is not a Turkic word. On jok, which is Schuessler's palatal glide, the frame is y…k plus l/r and admits yüklüg “laden” and yokla- “to rise, ascend”, neither of which suits an office. What cannot be tested here. The Chinese sources gloss 撑犁 and 孤塗 and say nothing about 谷蠡, so this row carries no semantic constraint at all, only the rank of the office: the 谷蠡王 of the Left and Right stood among the four highest, paired with the Wise Kings. The choice among the candidates therefore rests on the epithet argument that §S1.3 names as this supplement's main weakness, and the reading is offered as permitted rather than confirmed.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper. The reading takes the first of the three tabulated readings of 谷; on the lok reading no Turkic word can fill the first syllable at all. No Chinese gloss exists for this item, so nothing tests the reading

note: 當 tɑŋ → ton: direct, with the -ŋ coda written. 戶 gɑᴮ → ga: a velar onset, direct. Both characters do work, and the pair is the standard device for writing a medial nasal-plus-velar: in the Sanskrit corpus every source word with a medial ŋg or ŋk is written exactly this way, a -ŋ coda followed by a velar onset: 13 cases of 13, as in 央具梨 for aṅguli, 商羯羅 for śaṅkara, 鴦耆羅 for aṅgiras. Phonetically this is among the least demanding readings in the file: nothing inserted, no coda discarded, no character left over. The vowels are free as always, so Tonga, Tunga and Tanga are equally available. tonga “Siberian tiger, leopard” is the word in the name of the epic hero Alp Er Tonga. Big-cat epithets are a persistent Turkic pattern: Alp Arslan (arslan, lion), Baybars (bars, a large cat). Note that a search of the two lexicons on this frame does not return tonga itself; what it returns is tanuk “witness”, tañuk “a gift presented to a khan” and tünek “prison”, of which the second belongs to court vocabulary.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 骨 kuət → kut: default velar onset with the -t coda written, the tightest single syllable in this supplement. 都 tɑ then begins with the same dental, and Table 8 of the paper measures what that means: at a junction where a written coda is followed by the same-place onset, the source word carries that consonant once rather than twice in 121 of 140 cases (86%). So 骨都 transcribes kuta, not kutta. 侯 go → -k closes it, a Later Han voiced g- standing for a source k more often than for a source g. kut is “kut, uğur, devlet, baht, talih, saadet” in Kāşgarî (heavenly favour, fortune, sovereign grace) and Clauson records the verb kutad- “to be blessed”, the stem behind the Kutadgu Bilig. Kutak itself is not attested: it would be a deverbal or diminutive formation in -(A)k on that stem, which is a live suffix but not one witnessed on this word. Compare Qutalmış, ancestor of the Seljuks of Rum. Note also that kut is the Turkic candidate for 孤塗, where the Chinese gloss 子 “son” fits the Yeniseian proposal better and not this one.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

proposed_sense: the striker; from çak- ‘to strike fire, to strike a blow’
note: 且 tsɑᴮ → ça: ts- for a source affricate is a minority spelling but an attested one, 15% in the Sanskrit corpus and 9% in Ligeti, against a tś- character as the default at 37%. 渠 gɨɑ → ka: a Later Han voiced g- stands for a foreign k more often than for a foreign g. Both steps are permitted by the measured correspondences. çak- “to strike fire from flint, to sting, to slander”, which Clauson describes as onomatopoeic in character and of violent action, physical or mental. No çaka headword exists in Kāşgarî, the Codex or Clauson, only the verb and its derivatives çakmak, çakır, çakılmak, so Çaka would have to be the -A converb of that stem, and a bare converb serving as an office title is not a demonstrable pattern. The 11th-century emir Çaka Bey of Smyrna (Byzantine Τζαχᾶς, fl. 1081–93) shows that çak- could yield a personal name, but that is a personal name set against a title. The Chinese sources do not record what the office of 且渠 did, so no sense can be tested against a gloss.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 徑 keŋᶜ → kıng: default velar onset with the -ŋ coda written. 路 lɑᶜ → ra: a Chinese l- for a source r-, the direction those counts show in 12 of 14 attestations. The Turkic word's final -k is not written, which Table 7 of the paper licenses at 30%. Not our reading. Friedrich Hirth compared 徑路 with Turkic kıŋrak in The Ancient History of China to the End of the Chóu Dynasty (1908), pp. 65–70, calling it the oldest Turkish word on record. Kāşgarî glosses kıñrak as a knife like a butcher's cleaver, for cutting meat and dough, and the Chinese sources describe 徑路 as a blade used in oath-taking, so gloss and referent agree across unconnected sources. Turkic origin, on Clauson's analysis. Clauson derives kıŋra:k as a deverbal noun from an unattested *kıŋra:-, denominal from kıñır, in the sense of something curved or something that cuts crookedly, so the word is motivated inside Turkic by the standard authority rather than by us. Kāşgarî's index carries the same family (kıñru “askew”, kañrak “palate”, koñur- “to wrench, bend back”), and the Codex glosses Kingir as curvus. Clauson also records the word alive in Teleut as kıŋırak and Kirghiz kıŋarak / kıŋırak, a rough two-edged knife for cutting felt and scraping hides. Two cautions. Kāşgarî's text at III 382 reads kırpa:k, corrected in the margin to kıŋra:k, so the form rests on an emendation; and of the family it is kıñır that fits the transcription exactly, while kıñrak, the member meaning a knife, needs the unwritten final -k allowed at 30%. Iranian origin. The object has also been derived from an Iranian word for a short sword, the akinakes type, historically plausible, since the Xiongnu's western neighbors were Iranian-speaking. But 路 is a liquid-onset character, so the channel requires a liquid in second position, and the akinakes frame (k–n–k) has none. As stated, that account fails on the frame. Two cautions there too: we have not seen the exact Iranian etymon its proponents advance, and the channel shows what a transcription permits, never what it requires. §9.1 of the paper sets both origins out.
status: comparison cited in the literature (Hirth 1908), not the author's; tested here, with a rival Iranian etymology unresolved

note: 服 buk → buk: exact, including the written -k coda. 匿 ṇɨk → nik: retroflex ṇ for n is routine and the second -k is also written. This is the closest fit to its own transcription of anything in this supplement: no segment inserted, none discarded. A clay jar (Turkish küp). One of the few Xiongnu material terms the Chinese sources preserve, which is what makes it worth a reading at all.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 甌 ʔo → o: vowel-initial, direct. 脫 tʰuɑt → tuyat: the aspirated t- is direct and the -t coda is written; the only addition is the medial -y-. The border watchtowers, or the empty zone between Xiongnu and Han territory, for which the Chinese sources use 甌脫.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: 胡 gɔ → kü: the devoicing is normal, a Later Han voiced g- standing for a source k more often than for a source g; ü cannot be written and surfaces as o. 祿 lok → lüg: the -k coda is written. The consonant frame k–l–k is secure and only the vowels are free. külüg “famous, renowned” is an Old Turkic epithet of praise, recorded by Clauson; note that the form is külüg, not külük, and it is not a headword in either lexicon used here. Two objections stand. First, the Chinese-side record gives the meaning of 胡祿 as “quiver”, not a term of praise, though that gloss is itself marked low-confidence and chronologically shaky. Second, the reading the gloss wants is barred by the transcription: the one Turkic quiver word whose skeleton fits is okluk (Kāşgarî, glossed sadak), and it is vowel-initial, whereas 胡 carries a voiced velar. In the Sanskrit corpus a source vowel-initial syllable was written with a zero or glottal onset in 96% of 183 cases, and with a velar in none. So this is an item where the Chinese gloss names a target, a Turkic word exists for it, and the spelling rules that word out, recorded because a negative of that shape is worth more than a resemblance.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

proposed_sense: the ethnonym, from the first character alone
note: 匈 huoŋ → hung: direct, with the -ŋ coda written. 奴 nɑ is discarded rather than read, on the assumption that 奴 “slave” is a Chinese pejorative appended to the name rather than part of it. Dropping 奴 is common in the literature and what is proposed is only the vocalisation of the remaining syllable.
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper

note: A single character. 羯 kɨat → kıyat: the k- is default and the -t coda is written, so the consonant frame k…t is secure and only the medial glide is free. Fully character-anchored. kıyat, of flooding. The Jie are recorded as a group within or beside the Xiongnu; the reading is offered for the ethnonym only, and beside rather than against the standing one: Pulleyblank and Vovin read the ethnonym as *ket and connect it with Proto-Yeniseian *keʔt “person, human being” (Ket keʔt, Yug keʔt, Kott hit, Arin kit/qit, Pumpokol kit), which is the Yeniseian self-designation (Vovin 2000, CAJ 44/1, p. 91).
status: author's proposal; not supported by any measurement in the paper
